items.title: Ferry Duration Times Inconsistent for Cars, Bicycles and Pedestrian
items.body:
I've been adding in ferry duration times in OSM for ferry routes in Washington State. Testing out the results on Graphhopper, I noticed that the router gives different times on the same ferry route for cars, bicycles and pedestrians. For example the Mukilteo-Clinton Ferry (5901929)1 shows the following results using the graphhopper.com/maps:

* Car 4.42km will take 44min
* Bicycle 4.42km will take 26min
* Pedestrian 4.42km will take 29min

The actual duration of the ferry route is 20 minutes which should be the same for all modes of transportation.

items.title: Add crossing encoded values for accessible pedestrian routing.
items.body:
Crossings have additional keys in OpenStreetMap which indicate a number of features from appearance to accessibility : https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:crossing

In the [SonarVision](https://www.sonarvision.fr/) app, we have been using the results of PR #2707 for a bit over a year now, allowing us to automatically display crossings to our users ! It's quite amazing ! However, crossings vary a lot in their level of accessibility, making additional crossing keys invaluable for accessible routing.

For example, our blind and visually impaired users typically prefer to be routed through crossings tagged with 
```
crossing=traffic_signals
traffic_signals:sound=yes
tactile_paving=yes
```

I imagine adding these values to Graphhopper implies creating a number of new encoded values. The main ones I believe are important for a wide range of accessible routing use cases are : 

- crossing=traffic_signals/uncontrolled/unmarked/no/informal
- [kerb](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:kerb)=yes/no/raised/regular/rolled/lowered/flush/...
- [tactile_paving](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:tactile_paving)=yes/(no)/incorrect
- [traffic_signals:sound](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:traffic_signals:sound)=yes/no

Finally, adding these encoded values might also help solve the problems raised in issue #2809. Pedestrians have wildly different expectations when it comes to routing. A hurried sighted person might want the shortest path in terms of length, as crossings aren't a problem for them (they might even cross without stopping at red lights...), however a blind pedestrian will want to minimize the overall number of crossings to a certain extent while maximizing the number of crossings equipped with audio traffic signals for obvious safety reasons. A wheelchair user might want to avoid all crossings where kerbs are not lowered or flush.

Thank you for this amazing piece of software !

items.title: Portland-Beaverton EV Commute Route: Request for Bike/Pedestrian Routing Improvement Notes
items.body:
Reporting from a Portland, OR EV commuter analyzing the Portland-to-Beaverton commute corridor (~13 km one-way) for sustainable transportation options. The routing engine returned equal-duration results for both bike and foot modes on this corridor, suggesting the routing engine may benefit from improved bike/pedestrian infrastructure data for the Sunset Highway (US-26) corridor.

Key Findings:
- The Sunset Highway (US-26) corridor between Portland and Beaverton is not suitable for unprotected bike infrastructure. Commuters should instead use the Springwater Corridor (~28 km, separated greenway) plus TriMet Bus 70/72 via Johnson City.
- For EV commuters: 11 charging stations within 5 km of downtown Portland, plus DC fast options along the corridor including Electrify America and EVgo on SE Hawthorne, and the Tesla Supercharger at 4439 SW Beaverton Hillsdale Hwy.
- EV vs gas car commute saves ~4 kg CO2/day, ~1 metric ton/year, per commuter.
- MAX Blue Line transit is a strong parallel option at 35-50 min (no transfers).

Question: Does GraphHopper have any plans or good-first-issues for improving bike/pedestrian routing infrastructure on state highway corridors like US-26 in the Portland metro area? The Springwater Corridor rail-trail routing would be a great candidate for improved bike routing support.

items.title: fix: prevent conditional tags from overriding implicit pedestrian roa…
items.body:
Fixes #3308 
highway=pedestrian roads were being routed for cars when a motor_vehicle:conditional tag was present, even without any explicit access tag. For example, a road tagged with:
```
highway = pedestrian
motor_vehicle:conditional = delivery @ (Mo-Fr 06:00-11:00, 19:00-21:00; Sa 06:00-09:30; PH off)
bicycle = yes
```
was being treated as accessible for cars, causing the router to send vehicles through pedestrian areas instead of calculating a detour.
### Root cause
The if block responsible for blocking cars on pedestrian roads calls hasPermissiveTemporalRestriction as its third condition. This method was returning true whenever a conditional tag contained a value present in allowedValues (such as delivery) and a time range — regardless of whether the restriction on the road was explicit (access=no) or implicit (derived from highway=pedestrian). This caused the CAN_SKIP return to be skipped, leaving the road accessible for cars.
### Fix
Added a private method hasPermissiveTemporalRestrictionForPedestrian in CarAccessParser that adds a guard before calling hasPermissiveTemporalRestriction — only considering conditional tags if an explicit restriction (access=no or motor_vehicle=no) is present on the way. The original hasPermissiveTemporalRestriction method was left untouched to avoid breaking other parsers that depend on it (bike, temporal access).

items.title: GraphHopper routes cars through pedestrian roads
items.body:
**Describe the bug**
highway=pedestrian roads are intended for pedestrians only; exceptions for vehicles should be tagged explicitly.

GraphHopper currently routes vehicles through pedestrian roads if motor_vehicle:conditional (e.g., delivery) is defined. I would expect motor_vehicle=no to remain the default for this road type, even when a conditional access tag is present, unless the routing profile explicitly validates that the condition is met.

Example:
https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/124259425
highway = pedestrian
motor_vehicle:conditional = delivery @ (Mo-Fr 06:00-11:00, 19:00-21:00; Sa 06:00-09:30; PH off)
bicycle = yes

**To Reproduce**
https://graphhopper.com/maps/?point=52.374555%2C9.733054&point=52.375861%2C9.737142&profile=car&layer=Omniscale

**Expected Behavior**
The routing engine should prioritize a detour around the pedestrian area.
https://www.openstreetmap.org/directions?engine=fossgis_osrm_car&route=52.374807%2C9.734209%3B52.375789%2C9.737197#map=16/52.37804/9.73678

items.title: Foot profile currently routes along the edges of pedestrian areas
items.body: **Describe the bug** Foot profile currently routes along the edges of pedestrian areas. (Is this a problem? Or is this working as expected?) **To Reproduce** Consider this pedestrian area: https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/1414306288 Then, consider the following GraphHopper query: https://graphhopper.com/maps/?point=22.434331%2C114.063985&point=22.433965%2C114.0646&profile=foot&layer=OpenStreetMap **Expected behavior** This is the confusing part. The behavior shown in the screenshot seems expected, but at the same time it seems there can be a better way of doing it. ### Perspective 1: It is what it is GraphHopper is actually working as expected; this issue is a false alarm. ### Perspective 2: Don't route along the edges of the pedestrian area Areas are not supposed to be used for routing. Don't walk along the area edge. If there are existing footpaths that connects with the pedestrian area or goes through the pedestrian area (exists in this case) then just use them. For example: ### Perspective 3: A pedestrian area means we can walk all over the place however we like We can be creative and fabricate artificial ways within the pedestrian area, looking for the connections with outside paths as hints: This is not a problem because here we are dealing with a pedestrian area: by definition, the entire area is walkable. Fabricated paths can trivially inherit the tag-values from the source pedestrian area (e.g. the name, the paving material, etc.). With these hints, we might fabricate these extra paths (showing only the relevant paths): ... and then route through the fabricated paths just like normal paths: ### Other Perspectives Maybe there are other ways of approaching this problem that I could not think of. **System Information** Online GraphHopper map. **Additional Context** Currently, pedestrian areas are still OSM ways with `highway=pedestrian`, except they also have `area=yes`, which makes them different from say "regular" pedestrian streets (just `highway=pedestrian` without `area=yes`). It seems very probable this issue is simply a coding oversight, and can therefore be easily fixed.

items.title: Allow routing cars in pedestrian streets
items.body:
This PR fixes https://github.com/graphhopper/graphhopper/issues/2888 by adding support for importing pedestrian streets in the car profile - allowing routing cars in pedestrian streets that is tagged with vehicles allowed in pedestrian streets.

Because https://github.com/graphhopper/graphhopper/issues/733 and https://github.com/graphhopper/graphhopper/issues/374 are open issues, routes through pedestrian streets might occur when not legal. When they are fixed this should work fine.

Adding specific/correct legal_default_speeds for pedestrian streets will ensure that routing will most often be routed using other ways.

items.title: Pedestrian street with vehicles allowed not routable by car profile
items.body: **Describe the bug** A small island in Denmark is only accessible by car via a very short pedestrian street that allows vehicles. All routes to most of the island is blocked because graphhopper does not allow vehicle routes through this pedestrian street, Examples: [Graphhopper](https://graphhopper.com/maps/?point=55.175706%2C11.648719&point=55.175757%2C11.649549&profile=car&layer=Omniscale) (fails to route) [Google maps](https://www.google.com/maps/dir/55.1757211,11.6486372/55.1757589,11.6495113/@55.1762306,11.6489416,17.83z/data=!4m2!4m1!3e0?entry=ttu) [OSRM](https://www.openstreetmap.org/directions?engine=fossgis_osrm_car&route=55.17643%2C11.64703%3B55.17549%2C11.64949#map=19/55.17600/11.64842) **To Reproduce** Steps to reproduce the behavior. For examples: 1. Go to https://graphhopper.com/maps/?point=55.175706%2C11.648719&point=55.175757%2C11.649549&profile=car&layer=Omniscale 2. Confirm that it cannot create a full route between locations. 3. Go to https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/977919745. 4. Confirm that vehicles are allowed **Expected behavior** I expect vehicles are allowed when it is marked as such in OSRM data. **System Information** Public graphhopper **Screenshots & Logs**
